How was revolutionary nationalism different?

The period of assertive nationalism also saw the growth of revolutionary activity, particularly among smaller clandestine groups. These organisations differed from the open public campaigns of swadeshi and boycott.

Swadeshi organisers generally sought to mobilise people through economic choices, public meetings, educational initiatives and organised protest. Revolutionary groups, by contrast, included members who believed that armed attacks on colonial officials or institutions could help overthrow British rule.

Revolutionary activity

In the context of the early Indian national movement, revolutionary activity refers to clandestine political organisation and, in some cases, the use or attempted use of violence against colonial authority to bring about radical political change.

Not all leaders labelled Extremists belonged to such groups. Similarly, the existence of revolutionary organisations does not mean that the Swadeshi Movement as a whole was an armed movement.

Important organisations in Bengal

Anushilan Samiti

Anushilan Samiti developed in Calcutta in 1902, before the formal partition of Bengal. It became associated with physical training, nationalist organisation and revolutionary politics. Its activities and influence expanded during the period of heightened unrest after 1905.

The organisation should therefore not be described as having been founded only after the partition was implemented. The partition helped intensify an existing current of revolutionary nationalism.

Jugantar

Jugantar, also written Yugantar, was associated with a revolutionary nationalist group and a Bengali weekly newspaper that began publication in 1906. Figures connected with the publication included Barindra Kumar Ghose and Bhupendranath Datta.

Jugantar helped circulate revolutionary nationalist ideas. The newspaper and the political network associated with it were related, but the name did not refer merely to an ordinary commercial publication.

The Muzaffarpur incident of 1908

On 30 April 1908, Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki were involved in an attempted attack on Douglas Kingsford, a British judicial officer, at Muzaffarpur.

The attackers mistook another carriage for Kingsford's carriage. The resulting explosion killed Mrs Kennedy and Miss Kennedy, while Kingsford survived. The deaths were those of civilians, not the intended official. This distinction is essential to an accurate account of the incident.

Prafulla Chaki died by suicide after the incident. Khudiram Bose was arrested, tried and executed on 11 August 1908.

The Alipore Bomb Case

The Alipore Bomb Case of 1908 arose from investigations into revolutionary activity in Bengal. It became a prominent colonial prosecution associated with revolutionary nationalist networks and figures including Barindra Kumar Ghose and Aurobindo Ghose.

The case illustrates the difference between the public nationalist movement and clandestine revolutionary organisation. Both developed within the broader atmosphere of opposition to British rule, but they followed different methods and involved different kinds of political action.

Connecting the principal events

The central sequence of this subtopic begins with the 1905 partition of Bengal, which stimulated boycott and swadeshi mobilisation. The movement also encouraged national education and stronger demands for self-government.

At the 1906 Calcutta Congress, the principal nationalist ideas received formal support, but disagreements about their implementation continued. Those differences contributed to the 1907 Surat Split. Meanwhile, clandestine revolutionary organisations pursued a different course, as illustrated by the events of 1908.

The partition of Bengal was annulled in 1911, followed by provincial reorganisation in 1912. The Moderate and Extremist tendencies within Congress reunited in 1915. These outcomes belonged to separate administrative and organisational developments.

Final distinctions for objective questions

Term or eventCorrect identification
Partition of BengalBritish provincial reorganisation implemented in 1905.
SwadeshiPromotion of Indian goods, enterprises and self-reliance.
BoycottRefusal to purchase selected foreign goods or support colonial institutions.
National educationEducation developed under Indian direction and national control.
Calcutta Congress, 1906Session under Dadabhai Naoroji that supported the major nationalist programme.
Surat Split, 1907Organisational division between Moderate and Extremist tendencies.
Revolutionary activityClandestine political organisation, including attempts at armed resistance.

For statement-based questions, first identify whether a statement concerns a government decision, a Congress resolution, a mass movement or a secret revolutionary organisation. These categories may be connected historically, but they are not interchangeable.

Prelims focus

  • Anushilan Samiti developed in Calcutta in 1902; it was not founded for the first time after the 1905 partition.
  • Jugantar was associated with a revolutionary network and a Bengali weekly begun in 1906.
  • Muzaffarpur incident: 30 April 1908; Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki.
  • Intended target at Muzaffarpur: Douglas Kingsford; Mrs Kennedy and Miss Kennedy were killed instead.
  • Alipore Bomb Case: 1908.
  • Trap: Do not identify all Swadeshi supporters or all Extremist leaders as members of revolutionary secret societies.
